title: Unsafe or Unsound Practices, Matters Requiring Attention (final rule, OCC and FDIC, 91 FR 56004)
date_evidence: meta-article:published_time: 2026-09-01; "Published Document: 2026-17823 (91 FR 56004)"; "Effective Date / 2026-11-02"; "Dates Text / The final rule is effective November 2, 2026."
key_claim: The joint OCC and FDIC final rule, effective 2 November 2026, defines 'unsafe or unsound practice' for enforcement under 12 U.S.C. 1818 as conduct contrary to generally accepted standards of prudent operation that is likely to materially harm the institution's financial condition or present a material risk of loss to the Deposit Insurance Fund, or that already has. It sets a separate, lower-probability test for issuing a Matter Requiring Attention. The agencies invited comment on defining the likelihood by a minimum percentage such as 10% or 51% and declined to adopt one, holding instead that the probability must be more than speculative or merely possible. The definition applies prospectively only.
frame_summary: The agencies are arguing that codifying these definitions promotes clarity and certainty and properly refocuses supervision on material financial risk rather than on process and documentation, which presents a constraint on their own discretion as a service to the supervised.
verbatim_quote: The probability that a practice, act, or failure to act, if continued, will materially harm the financial condition of the institution or present a material risk of loss to the DIF must be more than speculative or merely possible.
verbatim_list: The final rule is effective November 2, 2026.
The definition of “unsafe or unsound practice” in the final rule applies to the agencies' supervisory and enforcement activities prospectively only.

the agencies invited comment on, but did not propose, more precisely defining the requisite likelihood under the proposed definition, such as through a minimum percentage (e.g., 10 percent, 51 percent)

title: Unsafe or Unsound Practices and Matters Requiring Attention: Final Rule (OCC Bulletin 2026-40)
key_claim: The OCC's transmittal states that the final rule creates a uniform standard for the issuance of an MRA to supervised banks, and that an unsafe or unsound practice must be likely, as opposed to merely possible, to materially harm the bank's financial condition or present a material risk of loss to the Deposit Insurance Fund.
frame_summary: The OCC is arguing that this is a codification exercise giving banks and examiners clear and tailorable definitions, so that supervision consistently prioritises material financial risk over process and documentation concerns.
verbatim_quote: The final rule creates a uniform standard for the issuance of an MRA to supervised banks.
verbatim_list: The final rule defines the term “unsafe or unsound practice” for purposes of both enforcement actions under 12 USC 1818 and supervisory activities

title: Agencies Issue Final Rule to Prioritize Material Financial Risks (joint FDIC and OCC release)
date_evidence: JOINT RELEASE / Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation / Office of the Comptroller of the Currency / August 27, 2026; footer "Last Updated: August 27, 2026"
key_claim: The agencies present the rule as establishing a uniform definition of unsafe or unsound practice for enforcement and supervision, uniform standards for when and how MRAs and other supervisory communications may be issued, and a tailoring mechanism keyed to institution-specific risk factors.
frame_summary: The FDIC is arguing that the rule is a continuation of the October 2025 proposal whose purpose is to redirect examiner and bank attention to material financial risk, which frames a narrowing of supervisory reach as a sharpening of it.
verbatim_quote: The definition will promote greater clarity and certainty regarding certain enforcement and supervision standards and ensure that examiners prioritize concerns related to material financial risks over those regarding policies, process, documentation, and other nonfinancial risks.
verbatim_list: In the final rule, the agencies clarify how the agencies will tailor their use of the unsafe or unsound practices definition and the MRA standard based on risk factors specific to an institution.

title: Prohibition on the Use of Reputation Risk by Regulators (final rule, OCC and FDIC)
date_evidence: meta-article:published_time: 2026-04-10; body: "The final rule is effective June 9, 2026."
key_claim: Effective 9 June 2026, the OCC and FDIC codified the removal of reputation risk from their supervisory programmes, citing the subjectivity of the concept, its inefficacy at identifying safety-and-soundness risk, and the potential for regulatory overreach and abuse.
frame_summary: The agencies are arguing that a supervisory concept they cannot define objectively should not be available to them at all, which establishes the principle that supervisory discretion is legitimate only where it can be written down.
verbatim_quote: Based on these authorities, the subjectivity of reputation risk, the inefficacy of reputation risk at identifying risks to safety and soundness or other statutory mandates, and the potential for regulatory overreach and abuse, the agencies have removed reputation risk from their supervisory frameworks and are codifying this change in relevant regulations.
verbatim_list: The final rule is effective June 9, 2026.

title: Shifting Sands in Supervision: What Are CAMELS Ratings, and How Are They Changing?
date_evidence: Shifting Sands in Supervision: What Are CAMELS Ratings, and How Are They Changing? / BPI Staff / August 20, 2026
key_claim: BPI argues the CAMELS Management component is the uniquely subjective element examiners use to direct bank behaviour irrespective of financial strength, and calls for the composite rating to be applied consistently with the agencies' standards governing Matters Requiring Attention.
frame_summary: BPI is arguing that the parallel CAMELS overhaul should strip examiner-driven judgement out of ratings in the same way the MRA rule strips it out of criticisms, which concedes that discretion removed from one instrument can survive in another.
verbatim_quote: Examiners use the uniquely subjective “M” or “Management” rating to dictate bank behavior: a bank that does not obey examiner mandates on how to manage its operations or conduct its business may receive an unsatisfactory Management rating, regardless of its financial strength.
verbatim_list: Establish clearer standards for the composite rating and ensure that the CAMELS rating framework is applied consistently with the federal banking agencies' standards governing Matters Requiring Attention.
notes: Used for the migration-of-discretion argument in the counter-counter. BPI is a bank-funded research and advocacy body; treated as Tier 2 institutional research with its position on the record rather than as neutral primary evidence. quote_provenance manually-verified: no sandbox network egress; page read during sourcing on 21/09/2026.

title: OCC and FDIC Finalize Standards for Unsafe or Unsound Practices and MRAs
date_evidence: September 10, 2026 / Skadden Publication (printed directly under the byline)
key_claim: The rule takes effect on 2 November 2026 and will have wide impact on day-to-day supervision; the FDIC has already begun reviewing and closing prior MRAs that do not meet the new standards; and the final rule, unlike the proposal, removes institution-affiliated parties from its scope.
frame_summary: Skadden is arguing that the rule genuinely raises the bar for examiner criticism rather than merely relabelling it, and that the criticisms which survive the clean-up should therefore be treated as more serious than before.
verbatim_quote: The FDIC issued a statement, “Implementation of the Final Rule on Unsafe or Unsound Practices and Matters Requiring Attention,” and shared that the agency has already begun reviewing and closing prior MRAs that do not meet the rule standards.
verbatim_list: The final rule, which takes effect on November 2, 2026, codifies the agencies' prioritization of material financial risk when exercising supervisory and enforcement authority and will have wide impact on day-to-day supervision of regulated institutions.
A notable change from the original proposed rule is that the final rule removes institution-affiliated parties (IAPs) from its scope.
notes: Practitioner analysis. quote_provenance manually-verified: no sandbox network egress; page read during sourcing on 21/09/2026.

title: OCC, FDIC Finalize New Bank Supervision Standards
date_evidence: meta-oni_display_date: September 08, 2026; also printed in the body directly under the headline: "September 08, 2026"
key_claim: Supervisory recommendations are abolished and the FDIC's matters requiring board attention are eliminated, leaving examiners with MRAs, enforcement actions and citations of other violations; the statute itself never defined unsafe or unsound practice, leaving it to agency discretion; and the Federal Reserve did not join the rule.
frame_summary: Morgan Lewis is arguing that this is the most substantive element so far of the OCC and FDIC deregulatory supervisory overhaul, and that the Federal Reserve's absence from it opens a supervisory split between agencies.
verbatim_quote: The final rule also constrains the types of criticisms OCC and FDIC examiners can offer banks. Gone are supervisory recommendations. OCC and FDIC bank examiners are instead limited to more objective actions, including issuing an MRA, pursuing an enforcement action, or citing what the regulation terms “other violations.”
verbatim_list: The final rule eliminates the FDIC's use of matters requiring board attention.
The statute itself does not define what constitutes an unsafe or unsound practice, and instead this has been left to the discretion of the federal banking agencies.
notes: Source for the removal of the informal criticism channels and for the Federal Reserve's non-participation. quote_provenance manually-verified: no sandbox network egress; page read during sourcing on 21/09/2026.

title: OCC, FDIC cement drill-down on 'material financial risks'
key_claim: Jeremy Kress of the University of Michigan holds that the rule exceeds the agencies' statutory authority, conflicts with judicial precedent and undermines effective supervision, and should be rescinded by the next administration; FDIC Chair Travis Hill has said the agency is closing a large majority of outstanding supervisory criticisms that do not meet the new standards.
frame_summary: Banking Dive is arguing that the rule is contested rather than technical, setting the agencies' clarity-and-certainty case directly against academic and political claims that it disarms examiners.
verbatim_quote: In a Thursday LinkedIn post, Jeremy Kress, an associate professor of business law at the University of Michigan, said the rule “exceeds the OCC's/FDIC's statutory authority, conflicts with established judicial precedent, and undermines effective supervision,” and “should be rescinded expeditiously by the next administration.”
verbatim_list: the FDIC is closing or has closed “a large majority of outstanding supervisory criticisms” that don't meet new standards
